# Pfaffian and Hafnian Versions of Lieb's Inequalities with Applications

## Overview

In this work, the authors establish new matrix inequalities by proving pfaffian and hafnian analogues of Lieb's classical inequalities. These inequalities, originally formulated in terms of determinants and permanents of positive semi-definite matrices, are here extended to their pfaffian and hafnian counterparts. Beyond their intrinsic interest, these results yield a concrete application: an improvement to an established bound in the theory of linear polarization constants.

## Main Results

The central contribution consists of pfaffian and hafnian versions of Lieb's inequalities concerning determinants and permanents of positive semi-definite matrices. The pfaffian and hafnian are natural matrix functions closely related to the determinant and permanent, respectively—the pfaffian is associated with antisymmetric structures, while the hafnian arises in the context of symmetric structures and combinatorial enumeration. By recasting Lieb's inequalities in these terms, the authors broaden the scope of these fundamental results and provide new tools applicable to a range of problems.

## Application to the Linear Polarization Constant Problem

A key application of the hafnian inequality lies in the study of products of linear functionals on real Euclidean spaces. Specifically, the authors use the hafnian version of Lieb's inequality to improve upon a lower bound previously obtained by Révész and Sarantopoulos.

The problem in question concerns estimating the norm of a product of linear functionals defined on a real Euclidean space. This line of research is commonly referred to as the **"real linear polarization constant" problem**. It seeks to determine how small the norm of such a product can be, relative to the norms of the individual functionals—a question with connections to functional analysis, polynomial inequalities, and geometry.

By applying the newly established hafnian inequality, the authors sharpen the lower bound found by Révész and Sarantopoulos, thereby advancing the current understanding of this problem and demonstrating the practical utility of the matrix inequalities developed in this paper.

# Pfaffian and Hafnian Analogues of Lieb's Inequalities with Applications to the Linear Polarization Constant Problem

## Introduction

In a celebrated pair of results, Lieb established fundamental inequalities concerning the determinants and permanents of positive semi-definite matrices. These inequalities, which reveal deep structural properties of such matrices under block decomposition, have found numerous applications across analysis, combinatorics, and mathematical physics. In this work, we develop analogues of Lieb's inequalities in which the roles of the determinant and permanent are played by the pfaffian and the hafnian, respectively.

## Pfaffian and Hafnian Versions of Lieb's Inequalities

The pfaffian and the hafnian are natural counterparts to the determinant and the permanent. The pfaffian arises as the square root of the determinant of an antisymmetric matrix and encodes the same alternating combinatorial structure, while the hafnian generalizes the permanent by summing over perfect matchings without regard to sign. By exploiting these combinatorial and algebraic parallels, we prove that Lieb's determinant and permanent inequalities admit faithful pfaffian and hafnian formulations for positive semi-definite matrices.

The hafnian inequality, in particular, provides a powerful tool: it controls the hafnian of a positive semi-definite matrix in terms of the hafnians of its principal submatrices, mirroring the way Lieb's permanent inequality relates the permanent of a matrix to those of complementary blocks. This inequality is the key analytic instrument that drives our subsequent applications.

## Application to the Linear Polarization Constant Problem

We then turn to the real linear polarization constant problem, a longstanding question in the geometry of Banach and Hilbert spaces. The problem asks for the largest constant $c_n$ such that, for any collection of linear functionals $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_n$ on a real Euclidean space, one has

$$
\sup_{\|x\| = 1} \prod_{k=1}^{n} |\phi_k(x)| \geq c_n \prod_{k=1}^{n} \|\phi_k\|.
$$

In other words, it seeks a universal lower bound guaranteeing that the norm of a product of linear functionals cannot be too small relative to the product of their individual norms. Despite considerable attention, sharp values of these constants remain elusive, and improving the best known lower bounds is a matter of continued interest.

## Improving the Révész–Sarantopoulos Bound

Applying our hafnian version of Lieb's inequality to this setting, we obtain a new lower bound for the norm of a product of linear functionals on a real Euclidean space. This bound improves upon the estimate previously established by Révész and Sarantopoulos, which had stood as a benchmark for the real case. Our approach thereby advances the understanding of this difficult problem and demonstrates the utility of the pfaffian and hafnian inequalities as tools in functional analysis and the geometry of polynomials.

## Conclusion

By transferring Lieb's classical determinant and permanent inequalities into the pfaffian and hafnian framework, we not only enrich the theory of positive semi-definite matrices but also secure concrete progress on the linear polarization constant problem. These results illustrate how combinatorial matrix functions can be marshaled to yield quantitative improvements on open questions in analysis, and they suggest further avenues for applying such inequalities to related extremal problems.

# Polynomial Inequalities in Euclidean Spaces: The Contributions of Lieb and Sarantopoulos

## Introduction

The study of multivariate polynomials on **Euclidean spaces** and, more generally, on normed linear spaces, sits at a rich intersection of functional analysis, approximation theory, and geometry. Two names that recur in this literature are **Elliott H. Lieb**, whose work on permanent inequalities has surprising applications far beyond its original setting, and **Yannis Sarantopoulos**, whose research on polynomial and multilinear inequalities has helped shape the modern theory. Bringing their ideas together illuminates deep connections between algebra, analysis, and the geometry of Euclidean space.

## The Euclidean Setting

In a real or complex Euclidean space, a homogeneous polynomial of degree $n$ can be associated with a symmetric $n$-linear form through the process of **polarization**. This correspondence raises a natural question: how does the norm of a polynomial compare to the norm of its associated symmetric multilinear map? The constants controlling this relationship—the so-called **polarization constants**—are central objects of study, and Euclidean spaces provide the cleanest and most classical arena in which to compute or estimate them.

## Sarantopoulos and Polynomial Inequalities

Sarantopoulos made influential contributions to several families of inequalities:

- **Bernstein–Markov type inequalities**, which bound the derivative of a polynomial in terms of the polynomial itself, extended from the classical single-variable interval to the general setting of normed and Euclidean spaces.
- **Polarization inequalities**, where he provided sharp or near-sharp estimates for the constants relating polynomials to their polar multilinear forms.
- The geometry of **Chebyshev-type extremal problems**, connecting analytic bounds to the underlying convex geometry of the unit ball.

His work often reveals that the "best" constants are attained by highly symmetric configurations, reflecting the deep interplay between the algebraic structure of polynomials and the metric structure of the space.

## Lieb's Permanent Inequality

Elliott Lieb's celebrated **permanent inequality** originally arose in the context of mathematical physics and combinatorics. The permanent of a matrix, though superficially similar to the determinant, resists many of the tools available for determinants and is notoriously difficult to estimate. Lieb established powerful bounds for permanents of positive semidefinite matrices.

The relevance to polynomial theory emerges because the norm of a product of linear functionals—precisely the type of expression appearing in polarization and **plank problems**—can be expressed through permanents. Lieb's inequality therefore becomes a decisive tool: it converts a hard analytic estimate on Euclidean space into a tractable algebraic bound.

## The Synthesis

The confluence of these ideas is most visible in problems concerning **lower bounds for norms of products of polynomials** and in the computation of polarization constants for Hilbert and Euclidean spaces. Here one seeks to guarantee that a product of linear forms cannot be uniformly small on the unit sphere—a statement with a strongly geometric flavor. Sarantopoulos and his collaborators exploited exactly such permanent-based techniques, with **Lieb's inequality** supplying the crucial estimate that yields sharp results in the Euclidean case.

## Conclusion

The story of Lieb, Sarantopoulos, and Euclidean spaces is a fine example of mathematical cross-pollination. A permanent inequality forged in the crucible of physics and combinatorics becomes an essential instrument in the analysis of polynomials, while the concrete geometry of Euclidean space provides both the motivation and the testing ground. Together, these threads demonstrate how progress in one field can unexpectedly resolve long-standing questions in another.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a math paper proving pfaffian and hafnian analogues of Lieb's inequalities for positive semi-definite matrices, and applying them to the real linear polarization constant problem.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.**

In 1966 E. H. Lieb established a family of inequalities showing that the permanent and the determinant of a positive semi-definite Hermitian matrix behave supermultiplicatively, respectively submultiplicatively, under partition into diagonal blocks. In this paper we prove hafnian and pfaffian analogues of these results.

For a positive semi-definite matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}A & B\\ B^{*} & C\end{pmatrix}$ we show that the hafnian satisfies the Lieb-type bound $\operatorname{haf}(M)\ge \operatorname{haf}(A)\operatorname{haf}(C)$, together with a companion inequality controlling the mixed term $\operatorname{haf}(M)$ from above in terms of the diagonal blocks and the singular values of $B$. Dually, for the pfaffian of an antisymmetric matrix associated with a positive semi-definite datum we prove a submultiplicative estimate of the form $\operatorname{pf}(M)^{2}\le \operatorname{pf}(A_0)\operatorname{pf}(C_0)$ under the corresponding block decomposition, recovering Lieb's determinantal inequality as the special case in which the blocks are square. The proofs proceed by combining a Gaussian (Wick) integral representation of the hafnian with a positivity argument, and by using the exterior-algebra formulation of the pfaffian.

As an application we address the real linear polarization constant problem. Recall that $c_n$ is the largest constant such that for every family of unit vectors $x_1,\dots,x_n$ in a real Hilbert space there exists a unit vector $y$ with $\prod_{i=1}^{n}|\langle x_i,y\rangle|\ge c_n$; while Arias-de-Reyna settled the complex case, the conjecture $c_n=n^{-n/2}$ over the reals has remained open. Using the classical identity expressing the spherical mean of $\prod_i \langle x_i,y\rangle^{2}$ as the hafnian of the Gram matrix $G=(\langle x_i,x_j\rangle)$, our hafnian inequality yields new lower bounds for $c_n$ and shows that the extremal configurations for the polarization problem correspond precisely to the equality cases of the hafnian analogue of Lieb's inequality. In particular we obtain the conjectured value $n^{-n/2}$ for several previously inaccessible families of Gram matrices, and we clarify the role of block-diagonal structure in the extremal problem.

# Abstract

**Matrix Function Inequalities and Their Application to Polarization Constants**

We establish a family of inequalities relating four fundamental matrix functions—the determinant, permanent, Pfaffian, and hafnian—for structured classes of matrices, including positive semidefinite, totally nonnegative, and Gram matrices arising from inner product spaces. Our central results provide sharp lower and upper bounds interpolating between these functions, unifying and extending classical inequalities of Hadamard, Fischer, and Schur, as well as the permanent-determinant inequalities of Lieb and Bapat. In particular, we prove that for Gram matrices generated by vectors of prescribed norms, the hafnian dominates the Pfaffian in a manner controlled by a Cauchy–Schwarz-type defect, and we characterize the equality cases in terms of the geometry of the underlying configuration.

As an application, we derive new bounds for **polarization constants** of finite-dimensional normed and inner product spaces. Given unit vectors $x_1, \dots, x_n$, the polarization problem concerns the extremal behavior of products of linear functionals or inner products $\prod_{i<j} \langle x_i, x_j \rangle$. By expressing symmetrized products of these quantities as hafnians and Pfaffians of associated Gram matrices, we translate our matrix inequalities into estimates for the $n$-th polarization constant $c_n(H)$ of a Hilbert space $H$. This yields an improved lower bound on the linear polarization constant and recovers, as a special case, known asymptotic results while sharpening the constants in low dimensions.

Our methods combine combinatorial expansions of matrix functions, majorization techniques, and the theory of positive definite kernels. We conclude with several open problems concerning the extension of these inequalities to complex hafnians and to the setting of $L_p$ spaces, along with conjectured extremal configurations for the polarization problem.

---

*Keywords:* Pfaffian, hafnian, permanent, determinant, matrix inequalities, Gram matrices, polarization constants, positive semidefinite matrices

*MSC 2020:* 15A15, 15A45, 46B07, 05A20
